title: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Under domestication new instincts have been acquired and natural instincts lost partly through inherited habit and partly through human selection, methodical or unconscious, of chance mental peculiarities, usually with both acting together.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence, we may conclude, that domestic instincts have been acquired and natural instincts have been lost partly by habit, and partly by man selecting and accumulating during successive generations, peculiar mental habits and actions, which at first appeared from what we must in our ignorance call an accident.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Domestic instincts, their origin”. Scope: domestic animals (dogs, pigeons, fowls, rabbits)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selection on domestic behaviour is testable in several species. Partitioning historical change between selection and inherited habit is not adequately supported by current datasets.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare domestic breeds and wild relatives for behavioural phenotypes, genomic selection signals, and experimentally demonstrated transgenerational habit effects. Selection signatures tied to breed histories support human selection; inherited acquired habits would require independent evidence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Darwin's inherited habit mechanism does not map cleanly to modern inheritance.

Historical unconscious selection is poorly recorded.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open trait and genome resources can show that some domestic behaviors map to segregating variants, which speaks to selection on accidental differences. They do not measure the share due to inherited habit, which is half of the stated mechanism. The test is therefore informative for dogs and fowl and incomplete for the joint claim across the named domestic animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For breed-typical behaviors in dogs, chickens, pigeons, and rabbits, test whether alleles and selection scans account for the behavior, and whether trained habits are transmitted to untrained offspring. A genetic response to selection with no inheritance of training would support the selection half and weaken the habit half; the claim's 'both together' reading needs a quantitative split between the two.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Inherited habit is not a variable in gene catalogs; those catalogs record genetic variants.

Pigeons and rabbits are much thinner than dogs and chickens.

Breed history confounds deliberate selection, drift, and training.
